section.title: Suffering for Righteousness
section.sectionRationale: Peter gathers the household teaching into a call for the whole church to unity and blessing, then addresses suffering for righteousness directly: be ready to give a reason for your hope, and remember that Christ suffered for sins once for all. The passage rises to the letter's most debated verses on Christ preaching to the spirits in prison and the baptism that now saves.
section.thesis: Because Christ suffered once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God, and now reigns victorious over every power, believers can bless those who wrong them, suffer for righteousness without fear, and always be ready to give a gentle, reverent reason for the hope within them.
section.frameNote: Three movements: unity and blessing instead of retaliation, verses 8 to 12; suffering for righteousness and giving a defense, verses 13 to 17; and Christ's victorious suffering, the spirits in prison, and baptism, verses 18 to 22.

verses.text: Finally, all of you, be {{homophrones|like-minded}} and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble.
Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with {{eulogia|blessing}}, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.
For, “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech.
He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it.
For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

units.label: Suffering for righteousness, ready to answer
units.note: give a defense for your hope

verses.text: Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good?
But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken.”
But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a {{apologia|defense}} to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect,
keeping a clear {{syneidesis|conscience}}, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.
For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.
For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but {{zoopoieo|made alive}} in the Spirit,
in whom He also went and preached to the {{phylake|spirits in prison}}
who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.

And this water symbolizes the {{baptisma|baptism}} that now saves you also, not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,
who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.

homophrones.gloss: Of one mind, like-minded, sharing a common outlook. Peter heads his list of church virtues with it: believers are to think and feel together in harmony. It does not mean uniformity of opinion but a shared mind shaped by the gospel, the ground of sympathy, brotherly love, tenderheartedness, and humility.

eulogia.gloss: Blessing, the speaking of good. Instead of repaying insult with insult, believers are to bless, and in doing so they inherit a blessing themselves. The word turns the natural cycle of retaliation on its head: those who have received God's blessing pass blessing on, even to those who wrong them.

apologia.gloss: A defense, a reasoned answer, as one might give in court. Believers are to be always ready to give an apologia for their hope. It is not aggressive argument but a thoughtful, gentle account of why they trust Christ, offered with respect to anyone who asks. From this word comes apologetics.

syneidesis.gloss: Conscience, the inner sense of right and wrong before God. Peter twice ties suffering and baptism to a clear or good conscience. A clean conscience, kept by godly conduct, both silences slander and marks the reality of salvation, the heart at peace with God through Christ's resurrection.

zoopoieo.gloss: To make alive, to give life. Christ was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit. The word points to the resurrection life and power of the Spirit by which the crucified Christ was raised and vindicated, the same power in which He proclaimed His triumph and now reigns.

phylake.gloss: Spirits in prison, those held in confinement. This much-debated phrase refers either to the disobedient people of Noah's day, now dead, or to imprisoned fallen spirits from that era. In whatever sense, Christ went and proclaimed His victory to them, showing His triumph reaches even to the powers of the disobedient past.

baptisma.gloss: Baptism, the washing that marks entrance into Christ. Peter says it saves not by removing bodily dirt but as the pledge of a clear conscience toward God, and only through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Baptism saves as it unites the believer to the risen Lord, its power resting in Christ, not the water itself.

basic.context: Peter calls the whole church to live in harmony: be united, sympathetic, loving, tenderhearted, humble. Do not hit back when insulted; bless instead, and you will inherit blessing. Even if you suffer for doing right, you are blessed, so do not be afraid. Instead, honor Christ as Lord in your heart, and always be ready to explain your hope, gently and respectfully, with a clear conscience. Then Peter grounds it all in Christ, who suffered once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. He died, was made alive, proclaimed His victory even to the spirits in prison, and now reigns in heaven with all powers under Him. Baptism, like Noah's rescue through water, saves us through His resurrection.
basic.hermeneutics: Most of this passage is plain and practical, but verses 18 to 22 contain some of the hardest lines in the New Testament, especially Christ preaching to the spirits in prison. Faithful Christians have read these differently, and we should hold our view humbly while keeping the clear main point: Christ's suffering was victorious and complete, and He now reigns over every power. Likewise, when Peter says baptism now saves you, he immediately guards against superstition, it is not the water but the resurrection of Christ and the appeal of a clean conscience that saves.
basic.originalLanguages: Believers are homophrones, like-minded, and return eulogia, blessing, for insult. They give an apologia, a reasoned defense, of their hope with a clear syneidesis, conscience. Christ was put to death but zoopoieo, made alive, in the Spirit, and proclaimed His triumph to the pneumata en phylake, the spirits in prison. Baptisma, baptism, saves through the resurrection, as the pledge of a good conscience.
basic.typology: Noah's flood is the great type here: as eight souls were saved through water in the ark, so baptism saves through the waters of judgment by union with Christ. The flood pictures judgment passed through into new life. And Christ's descent and proclamation, and His exaltation over all powers, fulfil the hope that God's righteous one triumphs over every hostile force.
basic.christ: Christ is the heart of the passage: He suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God, the clearest statement of substitution in the letter. He was put to death and made alive, proclaimed His victory to the imprisoned spirits, rose, ascended, and now sits at God's right hand with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him. He is the suffering Savior and the reigning Lord.
basic.god: God is patient, as He was in the days of Noah, waiting while the ark was built. He is the God whose eyes are on the righteous and whose ears hear their prayer, but whose face is against evildoers. He is the God to whom Christ brings us, and who raised and exalted Christ over every power. He is just, patient, attentive, and sovereign over all.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 34 is quoted on loving life and seeking peace, and God's care for the righteous. Isaiah 8 lies behind sanctify Christ as Lord and do not fear. Genesis 6 to 8 gives Noah and the flood. And Romans 8 declares that no power can separate us from Christ, who reigns over all.
basic.oneStory: From Noah saved through the flood to Christ raised and enthroned over every power, God's story moves through judgment to rescue and triumph. Christ's once-for-all suffering brings sinners to God, and His resurrection is the power in which baptism now saves. The suffering church, blessing its enemies and ready to testify, lives under a Lord who has already conquered and reigns over all.

context.literary:
The passage has three movements, and each leans on a quotation or an image from the Old Testament. Verses 8 to 12 close the household teaching with a short list of five virtues and a prohibition of retaliation, then clinch the point with a quotation from Psalm 34. Verses 13 to 17 turn to the possibility of suffering for goodness and lean on Isaiah 8. Verses 18 to 22 give the ground for everything in a compact confession about Christ, with Noah's ark as the hinge.

The opening list runs in two pairs and a closing word. Like-minded and sympathetic speak of the mind and the feeling, love as brothers and tenderhearted of the affections, humble of the posture. The commitment to bless in place of repaying is not a separate virtue but the test of the whole list when it meets an enemy.

Verses 13 to 17 are built on a sequence of contrasts: who can harm you, yet if you suffer you are blessed; do not fear, but sanctify; defend, but gently; be slandered, yet be shown innocent. Peter keeps pairing the worst that can happen with the answer of faith. The conscience in verse 16 returns in verse 21, making a frame around the paragraph, so that a clear conscience begins and ends the argument.

The final unit is among the most compressed sentences in the letter. Verses 18 to 22 contain a single long thought: Christ suffered, was made alive, went and proclaimed, and is now at God's right hand. The verb 'went' in verse 19 returns in verse 22 as 'has gone into heaven', so the same journey that took Him to the spirits ends in the throne room. The Noah story is brought in as an aside in verse 20 and then explained in verse 21, so that the ark and baptism sit close together as picture and reality.

Within the letter this is the pivot of the middle section. Chapter 2 grounds Christian suffering in Christ's example; chapter 3 grounds it in His victory; chapter 4 will draw the practical consequences.
context.historical:
The believers Peter addresses were scattered across the provinces of Asia Minor, 1:1, a mixed community living as a minority. Slander was the daily weather: neighbors suspected them of disloyalty because they refused to join civic cults, of immorality because of garbled rumors about their gatherings, and of dividing households. It is the climate behind the phrase 'those who slander you' in verse 16. Formal state persecution is not what the text itself describes. It speaks of verbal abuse and social pressure, and the fire it will name in chapter 4 is the ordeal of being despised.

Peter's phrase 'do not fear what they fear' takes on a historical sharpness. The prophet Isaiah told Judah not to dread the conspiracy that terrified the people when the Assyrian threat loomed, Isaiah 8:11-13, and the early church faced the same temptation to take on the fears of its surroundings. In a society where status and safety depended on conformity, to refuse the crowd's anxieties was itself a witness.

The story of Noah belonged to the shared memory of Jews in the period, and it was elaborated in their writings. In the book called 1 Enoch, the sinful angels of Genesis 6 are described as bound and imprisoned until the judgment, and the apostles Peter and Jude both refer to angels held in chains awaiting judgment, 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 1:6. Peter's first readers would have heard 'spirits in prison' against that background, though the background alone does not decide how he uses the phrase.

Water rites were familiar too. Jewish converts were immersed, and the cults of the Greco-Roman world had their own purifications. Peter's careful sentence in verse 21 sets baptism apart from such cleansing: it is not about the body's dirt but about an appeal to God. Christian baptism was by now the public mark of belonging, and in a hostile city it was a costly one, the visible point at which a person chose Christ over the old loyalties.
context.canonical:
Peter's use of Psalm 34 is the first canonical link. David wrote it after his escape from Abimelech, and it celebrates God who hears the righteous and rescues them from trouble. Peter lifts verses 12 to 16 almost whole, and he does so to say that the blessing on the righteous belongs to those who bless in return for abuse. The same psalm appears in 2:3, 'tasted that the Lord is good', so the psalm is a thread across the letter.

Isaiah 8:12-13 is the second. The prophet is told not to fear what others fear but to regard the LORD of Hosts as holy. Peter replaces 'the LORD of Hosts' with Christ, 'sanctify Christ as Lord', so applying to Jesus a text that spoke of the God of Israel. It is one of the clearest quiet claims to His deity in the letter. The idea of the fear of the LORD driving out every other fear is also found in Proverbs 1:7 and Psalm 27:1.

Verse 18 draws on Isaiah 53, the song of the suffering servant, whose sufferings are borne for the unrighteous. Peter has already used that chapter in 2:22-25. Hebrews 9:26-28 uses the same 'once for all' language to say that Christ's sacrifice does not repeat, and Romans 5:6 and 2 Corinthians 5:21 give the pattern of the righteous for the unrighteous.

The flood story, Genesis 6 to 8, is the setting of the middle verses, and 2 Peter 2:5 and 3:6 echo it, with Jesus Himself using it in Matthew 24:37-39 as a type of the end. The angelic prison matches Jude 1:6 and 2 Peter 2:4.

Verse 22 draws on Psalm 110:1, the right hand of God, which Jesus applied to Himself, Mark 14:62, and which Ephesians 1:20-22 and Colossians 2:15 connect with His rule over the powers. Baptism into Christ's death and resurrection appears in Romans 6:3-4 and Colossians 2:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter's immediate goal is to equip believers to endure without bitterness. He knows that the instinct under attack is to hit back, to retreat into a safe silence or to be terrified, and he addresses all three. Blessing replaces retaliation, ready answers replace silence, and the lordship of Christ replaces fear. Each response is meant to be possible because of something that is already true.

He also wants them to see that their suffering is not a sign that God has lost control. Verse 17 shows the other side: suffering for doing good is within God's will. And there is a second reason to hold the line, which is that the reputation of the gospel depends on it. A slandered Christian who has behaved well and answered gently leaves his accusers with nothing to say, which is what Peter means by their being 'put to shame' in verse 16.

The Christ paragraph is written to anchor all of this. The readers feel weak and outnumbered, so Peter reminds them of what happened to the One they follow: He suffered unjustly, died, was made alive and now rules over every power. If the Lord's story ended with a victory, so will theirs.

The difficult lines on the spirits and on Noah serve this aim. Peter does not offer them as a puzzle to solve. He wants the readers to hear that the powers that oppose God have always been outlasted by His patience and have in the end been defeated, and that the ark is a promise that a small and threatened company can pass safely through the judgment.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is overwhelmingly prescriptive in verses 8 to 17, and the commands there reach every generation of believers without adjustment: be united and humble, bless the one who curses you, sanctify Christ in your heart, answer gently, keep a clear conscience. What does need care is the question of what the commands do not say. They do not say that believers must accept abuse without seeking help. Paul used his legal rights, Acts 16:37 and 25:11, and the call here is about the heart and the spirit of the answer.

Verses 18 to 22 are a doctrinal statement, and what is described there, the death of Christ, His being made alive, His proclamation, His ascension, is something that happened and is not something believers repeat. The line about Noah recounts a past event and draws a parallel. It is not a command to go and preach to the dead, nor a license to build speculative systems from a single verse.

The word about baptism describes what baptism does in the Christian life, tied to Christ's resurrection, and warns against a mechanical reading. It is not a teaching on how little or how much water is needed, and the verse says so by denying that it concerns the removal of dirt.

The practical application of the whole is that believers answer opposition with a Christlike spirit, rest in the finished work of the Savior, and neither fear the powers nor think of them as equals of God.

debates.question: What does Christ preaching to the spirits in prison mean, verses 18 to 20?

views.label: Christ proclaiming victory to imprisoned fallen spirits
views.case: Many take the spirits as the rebellious angelic beings associated with Noah's generation, now imprisoned. After His death and resurrection Christ announced His triumph over them, so the passage declares His victory over hostile powers, fitting the exaltation over angels and authorities in verse 22.

views.label: Christ preaching through Noah to that generation
views.case: Following Augustine, others hold that the pre-incarnate Christ, by His Spirit, preached through Noah to the disobedient people of that day, who are now spirits in prison. The point is God's long patience and the warning of judgment for the unbelieving.

views.label: Christ proclaiming to the dead of Noah's day
views.case: A third orthodox reading sees Christ, between death and resurrection, proclaiming to the departed spirits of Noah's contemporaries, whether as announcement of triumph or of their condemnation, without teaching a second chance for salvation.

debates.bearing: The views differ on the who and when, but all orthodox readings agree on the main point: Christ's death was victorious, not a defeat, and His triumph reaches even to the disobedient past. None teaches a second chance after death. Certainty on the details is less important than the clear message of Christ's victory.

debates.question: What does Peter mean that baptism now saves you, verse 21?

views.label: Baptism saves as it unites us to the risen Christ
views.case: Peter at once explains: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Baptism saves instrumentally, as the God-given sign and seal of union with the risen Lord, its power resting entirely in Christ.

views.label: Baptism as the outward figure of an inward reality
views.case: Others stress that the water symbolizes; the saving reality is the appeal to God from a good conscience and the resurrection of Christ. Baptism saves in a figurative or representative sense, standing for the salvation it signifies, never by the water itself.

debates.bearing: Both readings reject any notion that the water automatically saves. Peter guards against superstition in the same breath: it is Christ's resurrection and a conscience made clean before God, received by faith, that save, with baptism as their appointed sign.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb in verse 9 for blessing is a participle in Greek, 'blessing' in the sense of speaking well of someone, which is the same stem Jesus uses in Luke 6:28, 'bless those who curse you', and Paul uses in Romans 12:14. The noun at the end of the verse, a 'blessing' to be inherited, comes from the same family, so Peter plays one on the other. The act of blessing is the practice, and the inheritance of blessing is the reward.

The word in verse 15 for 'defense' is apologia, which in the New Testament is the term for a reasoned answer given in a legal setting, as in Acts 22:1 and 2 Timothy 4:16, and for the defense of the gospel in Philippians 1:7 and 1:16. Peter does not require a courtroom, though. He says 'to everyone who asks', and the setting is ordinary conversation. What is asked for is an account of 'the hope that is in you', not a debate about every doctrine. The sentence closes with two adjectives for the spirit of the answer, gentleness and respect, which are often not found in those who are confident in their case.

Verse 15 also contains a quiet but important substitution. Isaiah 8:13 in the Greek Old Testament says 'sanctify the Lord himself', and Peter writes 'sanctify Christ as Lord'. To sanctify the Lord is to hold Him as holy, treating Him as the one before whom all other fears fall away.

In verse 18 Peter writes of Christ 'made alive' in the Spirit, using the verb zoopoieo, which in John 5:21 and Romans 8:11 is used of God giving life to the dead. It speaks of resurrection and not of a survival of the soul. The pairing 'in the body' and 'in the Spirit' is a pair of spheres, the realm of death and the realm of the Spirit's life, and the BSB footnote shows that the phrase can also be read 'in the spirit', with verse 19 beginning 'in which'.

The verb translated 'preached' in verse 19 is kerysso, to announce as a herald does. That is notable, because the usual verb for preaching the good news is euangelizo, which Peter uses of the gospel in 4:6 and 1:12. Peter's word in 3:19 is the herald's cry, which can carry victory or warning, and need not mean an offer of salvation. The verb for 'went' is a form of poreuomai, and the same verb appears for Christ going into heaven in verse 22.

The word for 'prison' in verse 19 is phylake, a place of guarding or custody, and the word for the spirits is the plural of pneuma, used for angels in Hebrews 1:14 and for human spirits in Hebrews 12:23, so the vocabulary itself does not settle the question.

In verse 21 the BSB says the water 'symbolizes' baptism, translating antitypon, a word that Hebrews 9:24 also uses for the heavenly reality of which the earthly sanctuary is a copy. The next noun, which the BSB renders 'pledge' and a footnote renders 'appeal', has a range, and translators divide over whether it means a request made to God or a pledge given to Him. Either way, it is the conscience and not the water that Peter stresses.

typology.fulfillment: Peter says the water of the flood corresponds to baptism. In Genesis 7:7, Noah and his family enter the ark and pass through the judgment waters that destroyed everyone else. The same water that drowned the old world carried the ark. In Christ believers go through judgment safely, because Christ took the flood of it on the cross, and baptism is the sign that they have been joined to Him, Romans 6:3-4. The type falls short in that the ark was a wooden vessel for a handful of bodies, and Christ is a person who saves souls forever.

typology.type: The righteous for the unrighteous: the sacrificial pattern
typology.fulfillment: Israel's sacrifices needed a spotless victim to stand in for the guilty, and the Day of Atonement repeated every year, Leviticus 16. Peter's phrase 'the righteous for the unrighteous' picks up that shape and says that the pattern was fulfilled in one death. Hebrews 9:26-28 and 10:10-14 insist that it was 'once for all', which means the endless repetition was a pointer, not an answer. The type falls short because animals could not bear moral guilt, whereas the Son took it voluntarily.

typology.type: The imprisoned spirits and the defeated powers
typology.fulfillment: Scripture presents the powers of evil as held in custody awaiting judgment, 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 1:6. Peter says that Christ, vindicated by resurrection, has gone to the right hand of God with angels, authorities and powers subject to Him, verse 22. The correspondence is that of captivity and victory, fulfilled at the cross where Christ disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:15. It remains partly future, since the final judgment of Satan awaits, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: The suffering servant who is vindicated
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 53 pictures a righteous one who bears the sin of many, is cut off, and then sees light and is satisfied, Isaiah 53:10-12. Peter's sequence, death in the body and life in the Spirit, follows that outline. In Jesus the correspondence becomes personal and historical. Those who suffer unjustly can trust the same pattern, in which the shame is followed by honor, 1:11, and 5:10.

study.christ:
The passage is the clearest compact statement of the cross in the letter, and every clause matters. 'Once for all' says that Christ's sacrifice needs no repeating, in line with Hebrews 9:26-28. 'The righteous for the unrighteous' names the substitution: the innocent takes the place of the guilty. 'To bring you to God' names the purpose. Sin is not only forgiven but the way into the Father's presence is opened, a thought Peter shares with Ephesians 2:18 and Hebrews 10:19-22. This is the summit of the letter's teaching on the work of Christ, the more striking because it is placed in the middle of a section on what to do when you are slandered.

The passage also leads to Christ by the sequence of His story. He was put to death in the body and made alive by the Spirit, a pair that is repeated in Romans 1:4 and 8:11. The risen Lord then 'went', a verb that links the proclamation of verse 19 with the ascension of verse 22, and He sits at the right hand of God, where Psalm 110:1 placed the Messiah. In Him the whole realm of angels, authorities and powers is subject, as Ephesians 1:20-22 and Colossians 2:15 say.

It leads to Christ by lordship. 'Sanctify Christ as Lord' in verse 15 takes a text about the LORD of Hosts and uses it of Jesus, a quiet assertion that Christians worship Him as God. To hold Him as holy is the cure for fear, since Isaiah says that only He is to be feared. A believer who has made Christ the center of the heart has no room left for dread.

And it leads to Christ by example, because the conduct called for in verses 9 to 16 is the very conduct of Jesus in 2:21-23. He did not repay insult with insult. He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. The believer's patient goodness is not a technique for getting through suffering; it is a reflection of the Savior.

As for caution, the details of verses 19 to 20 are disputed, and a reader does not need to settle them to see Christ here. What every view shares is the Lord's victory. The ark need not be pressed into every detail of the cross; Peter himself draws only one line of correspondence, water that saves, and says that its power lies in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who watches. 'The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer.' This is quoted from Psalm 34, and Peter places it right where believers feel unseen. God's attention is not a vague benevolence; it has eyes and ears, and the same text says that His face is against those who do evil. He sees, hears and acts.

He is a God of patience. Verse 20 says that God 'waited patiently' in the days of Noah while the ark was being built, and the same patience is described in 2 Peter 3:9. The delay of judgment is not indifference. It was a long invitation, and the ark stood as a public sermon. The same God is patient now, and Peter's readers can interpret the delay in their own rescue as mercy and not abandonment.

He is a God who judges. The disobedient of Noah's day perished, and the ark's survivors were few, only eight. Peter does not soften this. Divine patience and divine justice are not alternatives; they are two aspects of one character. The same flood that judged the world saved the family in the ark, so the waters speak of both.

He is the God who saves through a substitute. Verse 18 is the gospel in miniature, and it makes clear that the way to God was opened by God's own provision. The Father gave the Son, the Son gave Himself, and the Spirit gave life. There is a Trinitarian shape to the verse: Christ, the Spirit, God, and the resurrection of the Son all appear within a few lines.

He is sovereign over the powers. Verse 22 says the angels, authorities and powers are subject to Christ. The forces that terrify the readers, whether human rulers or spiritual enemies, are under His feet. This is why Peter can say 'who can harm you?' without pretending that nothing can hurt.

He is the God who permits suffering within His will. Verse 17 does not say suffering is good; it says that it can be God's will, and that it is better to suffer for goodness than for evil. This is a hard word, held in tension with His watchfulness and His care.

For worship, the passage leads us to bless where we would curse, because we have been blessed, and to give our best answer to those who ask in the confidence that our Lord holds every power in His hand.

crossReferences.note: David's song of deliverance, quoted almost word for word in verses 10 to 12. Peter chooses it because it describes the person who guards the tongue and pursues peace and then promises that God's eyes and ears attend such a person. It also shows that Peter's counsel is not novel but is how the righteous have always lived.

The prophet is told not to fear what the people fear but to regard the LORD of Hosts as holy. Peter writes 'Christ as Lord' in place of the LORD of Hosts. The link shows that sanctifying Jesus in the heart is the remedy for fear, and that Peter treats Him as the God of Isaiah.

God shuts Noah's family into the ark when the flood comes. The text tells us that eight went in, which Peter echoes with 'only eight souls'. It is the historical anchor for the lines about the water that saved and judged in a single stroke.

The same apostle speaks of angels who sinned being held in chains of darkness for judgment, and of Noah as one of eight preserved. These verses show that the angelic prison and Noah belong together in Peter's mind, and offer help in reading the spirits of 3:19.

Angels who left their proper dwelling are kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for the day of judgment. The language of prison and custody parallels Peter's phrase and is one reason many readers connect the spirits in prison with fallen angels.

Christ has appeared once for all to do away with sin by His sacrifice, and He will appear a second time to bring salvation. This is the fullest commentary on 'once for all' in verse 18, setting the single sacrifice against the repeated offerings of the old order.

Those baptized into Christ were baptized into His death, buried with Him and raised to walk in new life. It explains why Peter ties baptism to the resurrection of Jesus Christ and not to the water, and it shows that Paul and Peter speak with one voice.

At the cross Christ disarmed the powers and authorities and triumphed over them. This is the parallel to verse 22, where angels, authorities and powers are subject to Him, and it supports the reading that the proclamation of 3:19 is a proclamation of victory.

God raised Christ and seated Him at His right hand far above all rule, authority, power and dominion. Peter's last verse is a short version of this, and the match in vocabulary shows how widely the early church confessed the lordship of the ascended Christ.

Earlier in the letter, Christ's own conduct under abuse is set out as the example to follow. The call to bless and not retaliate in 3:9 is this example put into practice, and the two passages together give both the pattern and the power for it.

study.oneStory:
The passage sits at a point where the story of the Bible runs back to the flood and forward to the end. The question the Old Testament raises again and again is how a holy God can live with a sinful people, and how the righteous can endure while evil seems to win. Genesis 6 to 8 gave a first answer in the form of an ark, a small ship passing through judgment, and left the question open, since the flood did not remove the human heart, Genesis 8:21.

The patience of God in Noah's day is one of several signs that He holds back judgment to give time for repentance. Israel's prophets spoke of a righteous servant who would bear the sin of many, and a day when evil would be called to account. Peter says that both have come to pass in a single event. Christ has suffered once for all, and the powers that stood against Him are now under His feet.

What this passage answers, then, is what Israel's story had been waiting for: a righteous sufferer who actually brings the unrighteous to God. It also answers the pressing question for the church: if Christ is already Lord, why do believers suffer? The answer in this passage is that He is Lord and has defeated the powers, and that the present suffering belongs to the interval between His victory and its full display. Peter is describing exile before the return.

The passage also sets up what follows in the letter. The next chapter will say that Christ will judge the living and the dead, 4:5, and the call to arm oneself with the same resolve as Christ, 4:1. The ark moves toward the final deliverance; baptism is the sign that the believer has already passed through the waters.

In the new creation the powers are not merely subject but gone. Revelation 20 and 21 show the old enemy cast out, the sea no more, and the people of God safe in a city where there is no more death, Revelation 21:4. The ark that carried eight is replaced by a new heaven and earth for all who belong to the Lamb, who sit with Him at the right hand of the Father, Revelation 3:21.

quiz.q: How are believers to respond when insulted or wronged?

options.text: With blessing rather than retaliation, since they were called to inherit a blessing.
options.note: Verse 9: repay evil and insult with blessing.

options.text: By repaying insult with insult to defend their honor.
options.note: Peter forbids repaying evil with evil or insult with insult.

options.text: By quietly withdrawing from all who oppose them.
options.note: The call is active blessing, not mere withdrawal.

options.text: By returning good for evil as those who have been blessed.
options.note: True to the sense, though the answer should name blessing and the inheritance of blessing.

quiz.q: What does Peter say believers should always be ready to do?

options.text: Give a gentle, respectful defense of the reason for their hope.
options.note: Verse 15: be prepared to answer, with gentleness and respect.

options.text: Win every argument against those who oppose them.
options.note: The answer is gentle and respectful, not combative victory.

options.text: Stay silent so as not to provoke opposition.
options.note: Peter calls for a ready, gentle answer, not silence.

options.text: Explain their faith when questioned, honoring Christ as Lord.
options.note: True and close, though the answer should include gentleness and respect.

quiz.q: How does Peter describe the meaning of Christ's suffering in verse 18?

options.text: He suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God.
options.note: Verse 18: the letter's clearest statement of substitutionary atonement.

options.text: He suffered merely as an example of endurance.
options.note: He is our example elsewhere, but here the stress is substitution to bring us to God.

options.text: He suffered as a tragic accident of history.
options.note: His suffering was purposeful, once for all, to reconcile us to God.

options.text: He suffered to reconcile sinners to God once for all.
options.note: True to the sense, though the answer should include the righteous for the unrighteous.

quiz.q: What is the main point agreed by orthodox readings of Christ preaching to the spirits in prison?

options.text: That Christ's death was victorious, His triumph reaching even to the disobedient past.
options.note: Verses 18 to 22: however the details are read, Christ's victory and reign are the point.

options.text: That people get a second chance to be saved after death.
options.note: No orthodox reading teaches a second chance after death.

options.text: That Christ was defeated and imprisoned for a time.
options.note: The opposite: He proclaims triumph and is exalted over all powers.

options.text: That Christ now reigns with all powers subject to Him.
options.note: True, verse 22, and part of the point, though the disputed verses stress His victorious proclamation.

quiz.q: In what sense does baptism now save you, according to verse 21?

options.text: Not by washing the body, but as the pledge of a clear conscience, through Christ's resurrection.
options.note: Verse 21 guards against superstition: the power is Christ's resurrection, not the water.

options.text: By the water itself automatically removing sin.
options.note: Peter explicitly denies it is the removal of dirt from the body.

options.text: As the outward sign of the salvation received through faith in the risen Christ.
options.note: True to the figurative reading, though the answer should name the pledge of a clear conscience.

options.text: As a ritual that earns God's favor by being performed.
options.note: Baptism saves through union with the risen Christ, not as a meritorious act.

questions: Peter calls the whole church to be like-minded, sympathetic, and humble. Where is God asking you to pursue unity and tenderness rather than being right?
Instead of repaying insult with insult, we are to bless. Who has wronged you, and what would it look like to speak a genuine blessing over them?
Are you ready to give a gentle, respectful reason for your hope? How would you put into words why you trust Christ if someone asked you today?
Christ suffered, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. Sit with that exchange for a moment. How does it steady you when you suffer for doing right?
Christ now reigns with every power subject to Him. What fear or hostile force in your life shrinks when you remember who is on the throne?

translationNotes.note: Sanctify Christ as Lord echoes Isaiah 8:13; some manuscripts read sanctify the Lord God. Give a defense translates apologia, a reasoned answer offered with gentleness and respect.
Made alive in the Spirit and in whom He also went can be rendered made alive in the spirit, in which He went; the precise sense shapes the debated reading of the spirits in prison.
Pledge can also be rendered appeal, an appeal to God from a good conscience.
